panels.text: Double-entry bookkeeping records every financial transaction with equal and opposite entries, called debits and credits.
Each transaction goes into at least two accounts, so the totals of debits and credits must match. If they do not, something has been recorded wrongly.
That check helps catch errors and fraud. The books are 'balanced' because both sides must agree.

The Ragusan merchant Benedetto Cotrugli described the method in 1458. The Franciscan friar Luca Pacioli, a collaborator of Leonardo da Vinci, first codified it in a mathematics textbook published in Venice in 1494.

claims.quote: The purpose of double-entry bookkeeping is to maintain accuracy in financial records and allow detection of errors or fraud.
